title: Chapter 204 – The Keeper of the First Terrace
html:
[Terrace One, the Garden of Lamps – Hua]

The woman in the gray gown does not come down to meet them. She waits at the top of the stair with her hands folded, and by the time Hua has climbed the ninety steps she has had a long moment to decide what she thinks.

She thinks the woman is afraid.

It is a small thing, but she has learned to see it. It shows in the set of the shoulders, which are held too square, and in the way the fingers lock over each other like two people refusing to let go. The woman is perhaps fifty, broad-faced and weathered, with gray streaks in a thick brown braid and a gardener's callused hands. She wears an apron over her gown, stained green at the hem. There is soil under her nails. And she is looking at the four who have come up her stair, the thin tired man with the staff, the mute girl, the scarred woman with the bandaged hand, the small bronze beast on the man's shoulder, as though she is seeing ghosts walk out of a wall.

"You came," she says.

Her voice is rough and low. It trembles on the last word.

"We came," says Jian.

"I thought you would not." She swallows. "My grandmother thought you would not. She kept the lamps for forty years and told us every night that the Keystone would come, and we believed her, and then we stopped." A laugh with no breath in it. "I am sorry. I am not saying this well. I rehearsed it."

"You did not need to."

"I did." She unlocks her hands, at last, and wipes them on her apron. "My name is Maren. I am the Keeper of the First Terrace. And you are very welcome."

* * *

Hua has walked through a great many gardens in the last two weeks, and none of them has looked like this.

The hillside rises in rings, nine of them, each cut into the slope like the step of a giant's stair. Every ring is a narrow terrace of black soil, hedged with low stone and planted in neat rows. There are beans, and barley, and a kind of pale blue flower she cannot name. Between the rows run channels of running water, bright as quicksilver, and at the end of every channel hangs a lamp. They are everywhere. Hundreds of them, hung on iron hooks from posts and trellises, each a small clay vessel with a flame the color of honey. They burn without smoke. They have burned, Maren says, for six hundred and thirty-one years.

"Who lights them?" Hua asks.

"We do. Every dusk." Maren walks ahead, her braid swinging. "There are four hundred households on the Terrace. Each keeps ten lamps. If a lamp goes out, the Terrace is shamed, and the family is fed last at the Harvest Feast."

"And if a lamp goes out and the family is not at fault?"

"Then the lamp is mended." A glance over her shoulder. "We are not cruel."

"I did not say you were."

"You were thinking it." The weathered face is almost smiling. "Everyone does. The first visitors from the Third Terrace said so. They said, you keep lamps for the dead? And we said, we keep lamps for those who might come."

"Might come."

"The Keystone. The Warden. Any who hold the Ring." She slows. "We were told they would. It is the oldest teaching we have. Keep the lamps. They will come up the stair."

Hua stops.

Maren turns. The others stop, too: Jian with his hand on the head of his staff, Mo Yan with her lantern, Pebble stiff on his shoulder. The light of a thousand honey-colored flames lies across the terraces, and in it, for a moment, the gray-gowned woman looks like a figure carved on a very old wall.

"Who told you?" says Hua.

"The Stair-Father."

"The Tenth."

"We do not say Tenth." Maren's lips tighten. "We say Stair-Father. He built the First Terrace with his own hands, and he planted the first lamp, and he left his instructions in the Book of the Garden. Every Keeper has read it." She lifts her chin. "He is not a man to be named lightly."

"I am sorry."

"Do not be. You did not know." Her face softens. "Come. There is bread."

* * *

The bread is hard and brown and tastes of smoke, and Hua eats three pieces and asks for more.

They sit in Maren's kitchen, a low whitewashed room with a hearth and a row of copper pans and a window that looks out on the Terrace. A dozen children have gathered at the doorway to stare. They are all barefoot and sunburned, with gray eyes and brown hair, and they watch Mo Yan with the fixed unblinking attention of creatures that have never seen an outsider. Mo Yan, perched on a stool by the hearth, watches them back.

"They will not come in," says Maren, "unless you ask."

"Why?"

"The Book says guests of the Garden must be invited." She pours a cup of pale tea. "We have not had a guest in so long, I think they have forgotten how."

Hua looks at the children. At the girl in front, perhaps ten, with a missing tooth. At the little boy behind her holding a clay lamp as carefully as an egg. "Come in," she says. "Please. If you want."

There is a moment of dead silence. Then the girl with the missing tooth steps over the threshold, and the rest follow in a rush, and the kitchen is full of small elbows and breathless whispers. Mo Yan holds out her hands, palm up, to the nearest boy. He puts his own in hers with grave ceremony, and they stand there, staring.

"She does not speak," says Hua, softly. "But she hears. Be kind."

"We are always kind," says the girl with the missing tooth, with great dignity. "We are the Garden."

Jian laughs. It is a short surprised sound, and it makes the girl scowl. "I beg your pardon," he says. "I did not mean to be rude. I only meant that I have a younger sister who used to say exactly that."

"Did she mean it?"

"Not always."

"We do," says the girl. She lifts her chin. "We have to. The lamps would go out."

* * *

It is Maren who explains the Terraces, over the second pot of tea, with a charcoal stick and the back of a baking tray.

"There are nine," she says, and draws nine steps on the metal, a staircase rising from left to right. "The First is ours. The Ninth is the Stair-Father's. Between are the others, each higher, each smaller. Each is a garden. Each has its Keeper. And each is a door."

"A door to what?" says Jian.

"To the next." She taps the first step. "We are the lowest. We keep the lamps that guide the way up. The Second Terrace is higher, drier, colder. They keep the bells. The Third keeps the fire. The Fourth..." She hesitates. "The Fourth we do not talk about."

"Why not?"

"Because no one has come down from it in two hundred years."

The kitchen is very quiet. The children have gone still, listening.

"And you?" Jian says. "How do you come to be here?"

"We were the first." Maren sets down the charcoal. "The Founders' people, when they went up, were the strongest, the cleverest, the best of the Hall. They built the Terraces to hold the road. They left the rest of us below, in the lowest ring, to keep the lamps." Her mouth twists. "We were the ones who were not good enough to climb."

"That is not—"

"It is what the Book says." She says it without bitterness. "Let the weakest keep the light, and the strongest go up. My great-great-grandmother wrote it on the first page of the Keeper's ledger. She said it was the most honest thing the Stair-Father ever told her."

Jian is silent.

"It is not an insult," says Maren. "Not really. A lamp must be kept by someone patient. Someone who will not leave. The strongest are always leaving." Her hand drifts to the nearest lamp, a small clay thing on the windowsill, and her thumb brushes its rim. "We are the ones who stay."

"What do you keep the lamps for?" asks Hua.

"To mark the way." Maren looks at her, and her gray eyes are very steady. "Not for the Keystone. Not for the Warden. For anyone who comes up the road with a light of their own. The lamps burn so they can see the stair. If a person climbs in the dark, they fall." She tilts her head. "You do not know, do you? What the road is."

"Tell us."

"It is a ladder." Maren draws a small figure on the tray, a stick man, halfway up the steps. "A ladder is a way of getting from here to there without falling. The Founders built it so that people who want to go up can. And so the things that live above cannot come down."

Hua feels the hair on her arms rise.

"Things," she says.

"The Stair-Father's word." The charcoal stick snaps in Maren's fingers. "He said the Terraces are not just a road. They are a filter. Every ring is a gate, and every gate lets through only what is fit. The weak cannot climb. The strong may. And what is neither weak nor strong, what is other, is stopped at the next door."

"The Bloom," says Jian.

"I do not know the word." Maren's face is troubled. "He said, what must not be allowed above."

Mo Yan has gone very white. She is sitting on her stool with her knees drawn up, rocking a little, and her small hands are clenched in her gown.

"It is all right," says Hua, and puts an arm round her. "We are not going to let it through."

"No one lets it," says Maren, quietly. "That is why we keep the lamps."

* * *

In the afternoon the children take Mo Yan to see the lamp well, and Hua follows at a distance.

It is a deep round pit at the center of the lowest ring, ringed with stone, with a ladder of iron rungs going down into the dark. A tiny bright thread of fire burns at the bottom, so far below that it looks like a star. The girl with the missing tooth, who is called Sennet, kneels at the edge and drops a pebble. They all listen. Eleven heartbeats later comes a faint, silver chime.

"It is the First Lamp," says Sennet. "The one the Stair-Father lit. Everything else is lit from it. If it goes out, all the Terrace goes dark."

"Has it ever?" Hua asks.

"No." The girl is scornful. "What kind of Keeper would let it?"

"A tired one."

"We do not get tired." She frowns. "We get sleepy. Then we go to bed. In the morning we are not sleepy." She considers. "Except Old Berro. He is always sleepy. But he is a hundred and two."

Mo Yan has crept to the lip of the well. She lies on her stomach with her chin on the stone, staring down, and the little boy with the clay lamp lies beside her and does the same. After a time she lifts one hand and makes a slow sign, a fist opening like a flower.

"She says it is beautiful," Hua translates, softly.

"It is," says Sennet, with fierce pride.

The mute girl signs again. A hand held low, palm down, rising slowly. Then the same hand pressed to her ear.

"She says," says Hua, and stops.

"What?"

"She says it is humming. The same as the thing under the lake." Her stomach tightens. "Only warm."

The children stare at her. Then, very gravely, Sennet nods.

"It's the same," she says. "The Stair-Father says all light is one light. He says the Bloom is light that has forgotten how to stop. And the First Lamp is light that remembers."

Mo Yan looks up. For a moment her gray eyes meet Sennet's, and something passes between them that Hua cannot follow, a quick fierce understanding, like two sparrows on a wire.

They stay at the well until the shadows lengthen.

They are shown the stair at dusk, and it is not a stair at all.

It is a road. It rises from the top of the ninth ring of the First Terrace into the dark, a ribbon of pale stone wide enough for a cart, and it climbs, and climbs, until it vanishes into a sky that is not a sky. On either side, at intervals of a hundred paces, stand tall iron posts, each hung with a single lamp. The flames burn steady and gold. Beyond them there is nothing but dim blue air and, very faint, very far, a spray of stars.

"The Road of Nine," says Maren. "It goes to the Ninth Terrace, and the Stair-Father's door."

"How long?"

"A hundred years, on foot." She says it without humor. "Or one crossing, if you have the fare."

"The Ferryman."

"He used to carry us. In the first years. Now no one comes." Her mouth tightens. "We have never been up. None of us. The Book says the Keeper stays. The weak keep the light."

"You could go."

"I could. And the lamps would go out." She shakes her head. "I have thought about it. Every Keeper has. It is the oldest temptation. What is up there? Who is waiting?" She looks at Jian. "I do not think I want to know."

He studies her for a moment. Then he says, quietly, "I think you may be braver than any of us."

"Because I stayed?"

"Because you stayed knowing."

Maren laughs. It is a short, dry, astonished sound. She wipes her eyes with the back of her gardener's hand. "That is the nicest thing anyone has said to me in thirty years," she says, "and you are the first stranger I have met."

* * *

Jian asks the question after supper, in the lamplight, when the children are gone.

"How much does it cost to climb?" he says. "To the Second Terrace."

Maren sets down her cup. "The Ferryman takes a year per leg. You know that."

"I know. I am asking whether there is another way."

"There is the road. A hundred years." She watches him. "You have not got a hundred years."

"Ninety-three." He says it as flatly as a man reading a price. "And two hundred and thirteen days."

She does not flinch. "That is a very exact number."

"It is a very exact thing, in my case." His mouth twists. "I have been counting."

"Then you know the answer." Her voice is gentle. "You will pay a year at each landing. Nine landings. If you go all the way to the Stair-Father's door, you will spend nine years of your life."

"Eight. I have crossed one already."

"You crossed it on the Ferryman's account."

"I did."

"He will not do it again." She leans forward. "He is old, Head Lin. Older than the road. Every crossing he carries costs him. I could see it in the way he sat. He gave you the first as a gift. He cannot give you eight."

"No."

"Then there is only one other way." She looks at his face, and her own turns grave. "You can take his seat."

The room is very still. In the hearth, a log shifts and sends up a small shower of sparks.

"I have been thinking about that," says Jian.

"I thought so."

"I do not want to."

"Nobody does." Maren's voice is very low. "But he has been rowing for six hundred years, and he is tired. And you are a Nine-Ring holder, and so are your children. Between you there are nine seats. If one took the ferry, the road would be free. Not for a year. Forever."

"And the one who took it?"

"Would not leave the lake." She says it flatly. "He would be the road. As the Ferryman is."

Hua feels her stomach drop. She looks at Jian across the lamp. His face is calm, but she sees his hands, trembling in his lap, and she understands that he has already imagined it, down to the last grain of black water.

"I will not ask any of the Nine to do it," he says.

"No one asked you to."

"I know." He smiles, faintly, tiredly. "But somebody will have to. If we mean to use this road. If we mean to go up, and bring people back, and keep it open. Someone will have to be the boatman."

Maren says nothing.

"Not yet," says Jian. "But soon."

Hua finds the ledger by accident, in the small hours, when she cannot sleep.

She is wandering the kitchen in her stocking feet, with a candle, because the bed Maren gave her is soft and the dark is full of voices. The children are asleep in a heap by the hearth, Mo Yan in the middle of them. Jian sleeps sitting up in a chair, with Pebble on his lap and his hands twitching in his sleep. Maren has gone to trim the lamps.

On the shelf above the sink sits a book.

It is a large thing, bound in cracked brown leather, with a clasp of tarnished iron. It lies open, as if someone had been reading it in a hurry. She would not touch it, ordinarily. But the page is turned toward the candle, and the hand is a neat one, and the line at the top of the right-hand column catches her eye before she can look away.

Year 631. Third month. Visitor at the Stair. Yellow robe, gray hair, sword at the hip. Said he was of the Azure Cloud Sect, Elder Ye, and wished to see the Garden. Gave no seal. Was not admitted.

Hua goes cold.

She reads the entry again, slowly, with her finger under the words. Then the one above it.

Year 631. Second month. Disciples of the same Sect at the foot of the Hundred Stairs. Fourteen. They asked to climb. They did not know the road. I told them it was closed.

And above that:

Year 630. Eleventh month. First Sect party. Twenty-two. They came by the Hundred Stairs. They said it was a trial. They did not say who set it.

The candle flickers. Hua turns the page back, and back, her breath coming short. The entries run in a neat unbroken hand through years, decades, centuries. Disciples. Visitors. Elders. Seekers. Always the same pattern. A Sect party at the foot of the stair. A Keeper, turning them away. A note in the margin, in a different hand: The Sect does not know what it guards.

The Hundred Stairs. The Mountain Gate Trial. The test the Azure Cloud Sect gives every disciple, at the foot of the mountain. Forty steps recognized, she has heard Jian say, and the keepers secretly log extra readings. Step forty-two is a cradle clue.

It is not a trial at all. It is a staircase. It is the bottom of the Road of Nine.

"Maren," she breathes.

"I am here."

She spins. The Keeper stands in the doorway, a lamp in her hand, with her braid undone. Her face is calm. She has been standing there, Hua realizes, for some time.

"You have read it."

"The Sect," says Hua. "The Hundred Stairs. They—"

"They are our front door." Maren sets the lamp on the table. "They have been climbing it for six hundred and thirty-one years. They do not know where it goes. They think the top is a platform, and the platform is a trial, and the trial is a way of choosing disciples. They have never once reached the First Terrace."

"Why not?"

"Because they are not allowed." Maren's eyes are tired and clear. "The Stair-Father set a ward, long ago. Only those who hold a door signature can cross it. It has held for six hundred years. It has not failed once."

"Until—"

"Until the first moon of this year." The Keeper's voice is level. "When a man in a gray silk gown walked up the Hundred Stairs with a seal in his sleeve, and the ward opened for him like a flower."

Hua cannot breathe.

The thought arrives all at once, cold and clear, and she does not like it.

The mark on my hand is the key. The Sect has had it for six hundred years. They did not know what it opened. They pressed it into wax, on letters and contracts and the foreheads of dead Elders, and never once asked why. She curls her fingers over the pale ring. And now there is a woman who carries it in her skin, who has been awake for a month, and who does not even know how many doors she can open.

She is not the only key. She understands that, too. A seal is a copy. A copy can be pressed a thousand times. But she is the only one that can be asked.

"He needs me," she says aloud.

"He needs your hand." Maren's face is grim. "I think he knows the difference."

"Not as well as he thinks."

"Warden—"

"I am not the Warden." Hua lifts her eyes. "Not any more. I am Hua. I have a daughter. And I will not let a man in a silk gown take her mother's hand and walk it up a road she has not finished walking herself. Not while I have any say in whose hand it is."

Maren stares at her. Then a slow, crooked, startled smile crosses the weathered face.

"The Book says the strongest are always leaving," she says. "But it does not say what to do when one comes back."

Hua laughs, a short surprised sound, and finds that her eyes are stinging. The honey-colored lamps flicker in the window. Outside, a thousand small flames burn steady in the dusk, and under them, on the black soil of the First Terrace, the barley rustles like a congregation holding its breath, and somewhere far above, on a road that climbs into the dark, a single swinging lantern goes on.

"Ye Shuhan," she whispers.

"I did not know his name. I only knew the seal." Maren draws a breath. "A white ring. A gap. Nine spokes. It is the mark on your hand."

Hua looks down. She cannot stop herself. The pale ring glows faintly in the candlelight, and the gap in it trembles.

"He stood where you stand now," says Maren. "He asked to see the Road of Nine. I said it was forbidden. He smiled. He said that he would return, with an embassy, and that the Keeper of the First Terrace would find it in her interest to be hospitable." She hesitates. "I thought it was a threat. I did not know what he meant by the embassy."

"A hundred disciples," says Hua. Her voice is hoarse. "Twelve Elders. He asked it of the Wall, three weeks ago."

"Three weeks."

"Where is he now?"

Maren turns her head, slowly, toward the window. Outside, in the dark, on the topmost ring of the Terrace, the Road of Nine climbs into the blue night between its lines of golden lamps. And at the end of it, small and bright and very far, a new light has kindled that was not there at dusk.

It is not a lamp. It is a lantern, swinging, carried by a man who is climbing the road alone.

"Nine days," says Maren, softly. "He has been climbing for nine days. And he is almost at the Second Terrace."
